client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus at work — I'll be in the middle of something and just completely lose track of what I was doing, like my mind goes somewhere else entirely. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it's not like anything can change what happened.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief has a way of quietly pulling us out of the present moment, and what you're describing at work makes a lot of sense given what you're carrying right now. I also hear a kind of quiet exhaustion in how you're talking about this, like part of you is already tired before we've even begun, and I want you to know that's okay. You mentioned that talking won't change what happened — and you're right, it won't — but I'm curious, what would it mean for you if things felt even just a little more bearable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... if things felt more bearable, it would mean I could get through a workday without feeling like I'm just going through the motions, you know? Like right now even the smallest tasks feel heavy, and I keep making mistakes I never used to make, which just adds this layer of guilt on top of everything else. But honestly, I'm not sure I even deserve to feel better yet — she only passed three weeks ago, and part of me thinks I should still be in the thick of it.
therapist: That belief — that you don't *deserve* to feel better yet — is such a common and painful thought in grief, but it's worth gently questioning: who set the timeline that says three weeks isn't enough suffering? What you're describing sounds less like someone who isn't grieving enough, and more like someone carrying a very heavy weight while also judging themselves for feeling it. I'm wondering, if a close friend came to you feeling exactly the way you do right now, would you tell them they hadn't earned the right to feel better yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them to be gentle with themselves, that grief doesn't have a schedule. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm supposed to know better, or hold myself to a higher standard for some reason I can't even fully explain.
therapist: You just said something really important — you *know* the compassionate answer, and yet something inside you won't let you apply it to yourself, which tells me this higher standard you're holding yourself to runs pretty deep. I notice there's a kind of urgency in how you're talking about this, like it matters a lot to get it "right," even here in this conversation. I'm curious — where do you think that voice came from, the one that says you're supposed to know better or be stronger than everyone else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it came from my dad, honestly. He wasn't cruel about it, but there was always this unspoken message that showing weakness or needing help was something to be ashamed of, that you just pushed through and figured it out on your own. And I guess I internalized that so deeply that even now, sitting here talking to you, part of me feels like I should already have all the answers and the fact that I don't means I've somehow failed.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and it makes so much sense that a message absorbed that early — that needing help equals failure — would still feel so loud, even now. I notice as you said that, your voice got quieter, almost like that little kid who learned to make themselves smaller is still right here in the room with us. I'm wondering, what do you think it would feel like to let this conversation be one small act of defiance against that old rule?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I mean... I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but it also feels kind of... I don't know, too neat? Like, calling it an "act of defiance" makes it sound almost empowering, but sitting here still just feels uncomfortable and kind of shameful, not brave. I guess I'm not sure I'm ready to reframe it that way yet.
therapist: Thank you for pushing back on that — honestly, that kind of honesty is exactly what this process needs, and you're right to name it when something doesn't fit. Sitting with discomfort and shame without dressing it up as something more heroic is actually a much harder and more honest place to be. So let's stay right here — can you tell me a little more about what that shame feels like in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's kind of a heavy, sinking feeling in my chest, like I'm waiting to be found out or called out for something. It's not sharp, it's more like this dull weight that's always there in the background, especially when I think about how I've pulled away from people who actually cared about me. I guess I keep telling myself I had reasons, but the shame comes from knowing that maybe my reasons were just... excuses.
therapist: That image of waiting to be "found out" is so vivid, and it sounds like this weight has been quietly sitting with you long before your grandmother passed — like her death may have just made it harder to keep it in the background. It takes a lot to admit that the distance from people you care about might not have been fully justified, and that kind of honesty with yourself, even when it's painful, is actually the opposite of the person who "has no answers." I'm curious — when you think about one of those people you've pulled away from, what do you imagine they would actually say if you reached out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when I think about reaching out to someone like my old friend Dara, my first instinct is that she'd probably be polite but distant, like she's already moved on and I'm just this awkward reminder of someone she used to know. And then I catch myself wondering if I'm just assuming the worst so I have an excuse not to try. But even if she did respond warmly, I'm not sure I'd know what to say — like, how do you explain two years of silence without it sounding like an excuse or making things more weird?
therapist: You just caught yourself in something really important — you noticed the thought "she's moved on" and then questioned whether that story might be serving a purpose, keeping you safe from the risk of trying. That kind of self-awareness is significant, and it's worth sitting with. I'm curious — if you didn't have to explain the two years, if you could just say something small and true like "I've been going through something and you crossed my mind," what feels like it would happen next?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... if I actually said something like that, something that simple, I think I'd be terrified of the silence that might follow. Like, what if she just doesn't respond, or responds in a way that's polite but distant, and then I have to sit with knowing for sure that it's really gone? Right now at least there's still this small part of me that can say "well, maybe," and I'm not sure I'm ready to give that up.
therapist: What you're protecting there is hope — and that's not a small thing, even if it's painful to hold onto. I notice as you said that, there was a kind of urgency in your voice, like this matters more than you're maybe letting on, and that the "maybe" isn't just a safety net but something genuinely precious to you. I'm wondering — what would it mean about you, about your worth, if the silence did come and the friendship really was gone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... if she really is gone, it would mean I'm the kind of person who drives people away without even knowing how, like there's something fundamentally wrong with the way I connect with people. And that's terrifying because it wouldn't just be about losing her, it would be like proof of something I've always been afraid is true about me.
therapist: What you just named — this fear that there's something *fundamentally broken* in how you connect with people — that's a core belief, and it sounds like it's been quietly running in the background for a long time, long before Dara, maybe even long before your grandmother. I want to gently hold that up, because a belief that powerful deserves to be examined rather than just accepted as fact. Can you think of any relationship in your life, even a small or brief one, where you *did* connect in a way that felt real and mutual?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I sit with that question for a moment, and honestly my first instinct is to say no, there's no one. But then I think of this one coworker I had a few years back, Marcus, and we used to eat lunch together and talk about everything, and it actually felt easy, like I didn't have to perform or explain myself. But then he moved to a different city and we just... stopped talking, so I don't know if that even counts as proof of anything, or if it just proves that connection doesn't last for me.
therapist: What strikes me is that you almost dismissed Marcus before you even let yourself fully remember him — and yet when you did, something in how you described those lunches felt different, like there was a quiet warmth there that your words were moving past very quickly. That connection was real, it was easy, and it ended because life moved him to another city, not because of something broken in you. I'm wondering — what would it mean to let Marcus count as evidence, even just a small piece of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
